review.summary: AGENTLESS presents a simple, non-autonomous pipeline for repository-level issue repair: hierarchical code localization followed by sampled patch generation, filtering, and voting. On SWE-bench Lite, the authors report 82/300 resolved at $0.34 average cost, and introduce a manually filtered 252-problem subset. The results make a useful case that a structured, comparatively inexpensive pipeline can compete with more elaborate agents, though comparisons and benchmark analysis have important scope limits.

observations.claim: The paper gives a clear, implementable localization-and-repair design, with concrete prompt/context and patch-selection steps.
observations.quote: AGENTLESS addresses this by using a simple three-step hierarchical localization process: 1) localize to selected files; 2) localize each selected files into relevant classes, functions, and variables; 3) localize to code edit locations.

observations.claim: Ablations support the practical value of multiple samples and test filtering in the reported setup: results rise from 70 to 82 fixes, with filtering adding four beyond voting.
The headline comparison is not a controlled re-run of all baselines: reported results are drawn from external leaderboard or tool sources, and many baselines are closed-source.
observations.quote: For baseline tools, we directly use the reported results either from the official leaderboard [29] or from the tool’s official paper/repository.

observations.claim: The authors acknowledge that the agentless system struggles on issues without location clues; how to improve this difficult category remains open.
observations.quote: the closed-source agent tools perform better compared to AGENTLESS in the case where no location clue is provided.

unresolved_questions: Would the performance and cost advantage persist under a fully controlled, same-model and same-evaluation rerun of the competing approaches?
How robust are the reported results to alternative model versions, repositories, and benchmarks beyond SWE-bench Lite and the authors’ filtered subset?
The manual classification motivates SWE-bench Lite-S, but the inspected paper does not establish how consistently independent annotators would apply the categories or agree on the exclusions.
This assessment is based on the supplied pages; implementation details beyond those described, and any supplementary materials, were not inspected.
